NPR News
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican
Alaska Public Media |
By
Eric Stone
Published November 13, 2026 at 9:12 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Eric Stone
Alaska Public Media
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, has won the race for governor of Alaska and will replace the outgoing Republican. Here he's seen at a polling station at the University of Alaska Anchorage on Election Day.
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the small island community of Sitka, won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press. At 37, he'll be the youngest governor in state history.
Kreiss-Tomkins will replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. The state's last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002.
Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his "high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach" a centerpiece of his campaign.
Sponsored
He's said he plans to build an administration of Democrats, Republicans and independents and described himself at a debate as a "man of the middle." He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski.
Alaskans have had enough of zero-sum partisan politics, he said in an interview just before voting at a precinct in Anchorage on Election Day.
"I strongly believe people just want things to work, and want people to work together," Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Loading...
The AP race call came after over a week of counting votes, including those coming in by mail and from remote parts of the state. In the ranked-choice system the state uses, he faced three Republican candidates, including one backed by President Trump. Winning requires getting a majority of the votes.
Voters were also facing a question on the ballot about whether to scrap that unique, ranked-choice system. That proposal failed, according to another AP race call, keeping the system in place.
With Kreiss-Tomkins' win and others in the midterms, Democrats will hold 30 governors' offices across the country, up from 24 now.
Sponsored
Kreiss-Tomkins will take office in a state where voters have loudly complained that things aren't working as they should.
Rising costs and relatively flat state funding have forced schools to close and class sizes to rise. Already-high costs for food, fuel and housing have risen sharply, and a looming shortage of easily accessible natural gas near the state's population centers is threatening to push prices higher. And Alaskans have been migrating out of the state for more than a decade.
The Republicans in the race were Trump-backed business owner Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor.
Kreiss-Tomkins is set to take office at noon Dec. 7.
Eric Stone covers state government for Alaska Public Media.

NPR News
The role of a pilot during a ground stop, according to an expert
NPR |
By
Tyler Bartlam,
Patrick Jarenwattananon, Scott Detrow
Published November 13, 2026 at 6:38 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
The FAA has now lifted its nationwide ground stop, but when it was in effect earlier today, there were still planes in the sky, and pilots had to navigate the situation at a moment's notice with little information. Earlier tonight, when the ground stop was still in effect, I spoke to John Cox, a former commercial airline pilot and an aviation safety expert.
If you were flying a plane this afternoon, this evening, what would be going through your mind when you got this update?
Sponsored
JOHN COX: I think the first thing would be, let's try to find out what we can do to stay in communication. There are backup frequencies. There are other pilots that we can talk to. And those are going to be the first things that we're going to do. I'm going to look for data link capability through a system known as ACARS or CPDLC and see if I can get the necessary information via data link. So there's several redundancies built into the system.
DETROW: I haven't seen any indications from radar or from official announcements or from reporting at airports that they're doing what they did on 9/11 and making planes land as quickly as possible at the nearest airport. Is that an indication to you that they're not concerned about the planes that are in the sky or that they just think, keep them on the routes as is?
COX: They've said very specifically that the aircraft that were en route were going to continue to their destinations. They amended that later and said there might be some airborne holding. And these are at the major congested airports. One of the things that is becoming an increasing issue is the physical ground space to put the airplanes, so they - may be some diversions. But it says that they're not concerned from a security standpoint, that it is just the massive amount of aircraft in the skies landing safely at a place - at an airport that can actually handle them.
DETROW: Yeah.
COX: And so with there being very few departures, these airports are backing up. O'Hare, Reagan National in Washington are two that have said that they're really short on ground space.
DETROW: OK. I mean, from what we know right now, do you have any guesses about what the problem could be? - a problem that, you know, flights in the air are continuing, as is, as you just explained, but a nationwide ground halt? Like, any sense what could be going on here?
COX: No. I think right now, as any good investigator will tell you, in the early hours, the thing you want to do is gather evidence.
Sponsored
DETROW: Yeah.
COX: They're going to be looking for commonality between these en route traffic control centers because the system's designed not to have a single-point failure. And yet today, something happened, and we got a cascading of issues. So...
DETROW: Yeah.
COX: ...Where's the origin of that? How did it proliferate from one en route traffic control center to another? Those are the sorts of questions that they're going to focus on in the early hours.
DETROW: Can you just take a step back and help us understand how often pilots are talking to those regional air traffic control centers when they're in the air, and how much the air traffic control centers are communicating with each other about the routes?
COX: It's pretty constant. The - once you're in the cruise phase of flight, the communication level drops, where you're literally - you're talking to a controller, and you tell them your altitude, and if things are quiet and they want to leave you on your route, the next thing you'll hear - some eight, 10, 15, 20 minutes later - is to contact the next sector in the center airspace.
If, on the other hand, you're flying overhead a busy airport, and there's a lot of traffic, and there's a lot of clearances or routings that are being changed, then it can be a pretty constant flow of information to and from the air traffic controller. One pilot may not be talking to them all the time. There may be 15 pilots on frequency, and if so, one of those 15 is talking with a controller pretty constantly.
Sponsored
DETROW: John Cox, you have that classic reassuring pilot voice, as I'm sure you know. And I'm wondering - that makes me wonder how would you communicate this to passengers in the air if you had been piloting a flight tonight? What would you say? How would you explain it?
COX: I think I would explain it that we are experiencing some issues with the air traffic control system, that there are contingencies in place, and we are following them. We are guaranteed separation from other aircraft by following those procedures. Things are going to be slower, and they're going to be slower once we get on the ground at our destination. So I would ask them to be patient and to let the system work in the way that it's designed and that I would ask them then to sit back and relax and enjoy the flight.
DETROW: (Laughter) Last question. What are your two or three biggest questions you have right now based on the sparse public information we've got?
COX: Where's the commonality in the center? How could one problem proliferate between different air traffic control centers? Is it something that is new? Is there a new system that's been implemented? Are there common areas for fiber optic cables or anywhere? I'd be looking for commonality...
DETROW: All rig

Immigration
Judge rules Adams County violated WA state law by working with ICE
KUOW |
By
Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez
Published November 13, 2026 at 6:12 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
KUOW/Amy Radil
Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown outside the federal courthouse in Seattle on Jan. 23, 2025.
A judge ruled on Friday Adams County has violated state law by collaborating with federal immigration enforcement.
The state’s Keep Washington Working Act , passed in 2019, prohibits local law enforcement from asking people about their immigration status or holding them for immigration agents.
“Today’s ruling allows our state to continue building trust and confidence between law enforcement and immigrant communities as the federal administration undermines those efforts with its draconian policies,” Attorney General Nick Brown wrote in a statement announcing the outcome of the lawsuit.
Sponsored
A majority of people locked up by immigration enforcement have no criminal record. Amid concerns of racial profiling by law enforcement, many U.S. citizens now carry passports in their daily lives. Many immigrant communities, throughout Washington State and across the spectrum of legal status, have strained relationships with local law enforcement.
Immigration
ICE arrests surge at Seattle-area Home Depot parking lots. Neighbors are on the lookout
Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez
“This is not about politics, race, or immigration status,” wrote Adams County Sheriff Dale Wager in a press statement acknowledging the legal blow, “It is about public safety, accountability, and the ability of law enforcement agencies to work together to protect the communities we serve.”
The start of the lawsuit
The AG’s office initially launched the lawsuit back in 2025, after a man in the country without legal status was booked by Adams County on criminal charges that were later dropped. Instead of releasing the man, local law enforcement officials placed him on a call with federal immigration enforcement, and later took the man to the agents. The man was then arrested and taken to the Northwest ICE Processing Center. He was later released, and is pursuing legal status.
Spokane County Superior Court Judge Marla L. Polin found that those actions, and others, were in violation of the state's Keep Washington Working Act. Other violations, according to the lawsuit, included sending daily custody lists to federal immigration authorities, failing to adopt the state's guidance and failing to address yearslong complaints sent to Adams County from the AG's office.
In 2022, the AG’s office sent a letter to Adams County Sheriff Wagner and Prosecuting Attorney Randy Flyckt, raising concerns about their cooperation with federal immigration agencies.
According to the letter, county officials aided Immigration and Customs Enforcement more than 200 times between May 2019, when the Keep Washington Working Act took effect, and December 2021.
Sponsored
Education
Issaquah on edge after ICE arrest outside preschool
Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez
Since then, the Attorney General’s Office began meeting with Adams County to address those concerns.
“Over the course of almost two years, they did those meetings, said they were changing policy, said they were acting consistent with state law, and then, in fact, were not,” Brown said back in 2025. “[They] never once claimed that what they were being asked to do somehow violated federal law.”
Sheriff’s legal defense has ties to national group
Sheriff Wagner and others were represented by special deputy Attorney Joel Ard. Ard is with the Ard Law Group and backed by America First Legal, a law firm founded by Stephen Miller, current chief of staff of President Donald Trump. Miller is an architect behind the president’s mass deportation efforts. During enforcement actions, U.S citizens and immigrants have been killed. Thousands of unlawful detainment lawsuits have been filed, overwhelming courts.
Wagner said he plans to appeal the judge’s ruling.
“I respect the judicial process, but respecting that process does not mean we must agree with every ruling,” Wagner wrote.
“Our States continued pursuit of these policies represents, in my view, a misguided political agenda that puts ideology ahead of common sense and public safety. I believe these restrictions make Adams County and Washington state less safe.”
Sponsored
The lawsuit requires Adams County to fall into compliance with the Keep Washington Working Act.

Environment
Quinault tribe races against king tides to relocate coastal homes
KUOW |
By
John Ryan
Published November 13, 2026 at 5:03 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
KUOW Photo / John Ryan
A rock seawall, covered in surf-tossed driftwood, protects James de la Cruz's house, left, and the flood-prone village of Taholah, Washington, from the Pacific Ocean on Oct. 1, 2026.
The Quinault Indian Nation on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula has been working for decades to move Taholah, the tribe’s largest village, to an upland location, safe from rising seas and tsunamis.
In October, after the tribe got federal approval to install four modular homes, the first of 59 planned residences in a new neighborhood about a mile from the oceanfront village, it held a celebration, with speeches, gifts, and dancing.
Luvaila Smith, Miss Quinault Nation, scattered tufts of eagle down into the breeze while a group of men drummed and sang amid the homesites cleared from Sitka spruce forest above the village.
Sponsored
Residents of four homes along First Avenue — the village of 800 people’s most flood-prone street — are being given new homes up the hill. Their current homes, moldy and sitting up on cinder blocks, are to be condemned.
“I wholeheartedly don't want to move, but I understand the need for it,” Quinault elder and Army veteran James de la Cruz said at the celebration.
KUOW Photo / John Ryan
Taholah, Washington, resident James de la Cruz speaks at a Quinault Indian Nation groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 1, 2026.
Every winter, parts of Taholah flood as high tides and waves overwhelm the village’s rocky sea wall near the mouth of the Quinault River.
De la Cruz has lived on First Avenue, in the shadow of the sea wall, for 35 years.
“I wasn't too much afraid of the ocean, but when them tides come, there's three feet of water in my yard, so I had to have a boat tied to my back porch if I wanted to escape from those high tides,” he said.
Winter tides are coming
The tribe’s ongoing construction on higher ground is racing against the arrival of the highest tides of the year, known as king tides.
Sponsored
Those tides could be boosted to record heights this year by one of the strongest El Niños on record.
King tides are expected to hit the Washington coast around Thanksgiving, then again in late December and late January.
Part of De la Cruz’s home is 17 feet off the ground, on stilts that let him look out over the seawall at the ocean that he loves.
“How do you give up what I consider the most beautiful view in the world?” he asked. “I do respect the ocean and know that it can do damage. I’ll get out of here when I need to.”
De La Cruz and his neighbors along the First Avenue seawall are slated to get the first homes in the new neighborhood 130 feet above sea level.
“When we have the full-sized tides that come with the winter king tides, our street, our house, is just shaking for hours,” First Avenue resident Lia Frenchman said. “There's just so much power behind that water. It has the whole ocean behind it.”
Frenchman says people in Taholah seem most concerned about the risk of a tsunami suddenly putting the village underwater.
Sponsored
But the steady creep of rising sea levels has made the danger of inundation real as a warming ocean keeps expanding.
“The fact is, it did not used to flood every year like it does right now, and that's definitely climate change,” Frenchman said.
She says her home is never really dry anymore, with moldy closets that defy cleaning.
“It’s so clear when nature is showing you that you shouldn't be somewhere anymore, that where you're sitting at or where you're dwelling isn't OK, and we need to listen to that,” Frenchman said.
KUOW Photo / John Ryan
Taholah, Washington, resident Lia Frenchman stands in front of the seawall that protects her home from the Pacific Ocean on Oct. 1, 2026.
De la Cruz and Frenchman both say they’re grateful the tribe is giving them safe new homes, but they worry that they will have to endure more flooding before their homes are ready.
“I was hoping to be in a home by Christmas, but I guess that’s not a realistic thing,” de la Cruz said.
The highest tide of 2026 is predicted to arrive in Taholah just before noon on Christmas Eve.
Sponsored
How high any given tide reaches depends on the relative positions of the Earth, moon, and sun, but also on less-predictable factors such as barometric pressure, winds, and water temperatures. The worst flooding usually comes when multiple factors work together to pull water up onto the land.
Retreat leaders
Waterfronts around the world are threatened by rising seas.
Along with tribes in Alaska and Louisiana, the Quinault Nation has become a national leader in confronting rising sea levels.
“This relocation of our villages has been a priority of the nation for decades,” said Quinault Indian Nation Chief Operating Officer M’liss DeWald. “Our leaders had the foresight and understanding to recognize the impacts that climate change would have on our villages long before the federal or state government recognized climate change as an issue affecting residential communities.”
To protect its most vulnerable members, the Quinault Nation opened its health clinic at the upland site in 2007 and a center for seniors and daycare in 2021. A new K-12 school is currently under construction.
KUOW Photo / John Ryan

Food
L’Oursin celebrates 10 years of ‘de-fancifying’ French dining
KUOW |
By
Brandi Fullwood
Published November 13, 2026 at 4:47 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Brandi Fullwood
KUOW
L'Oursin's Pate de Campagne cocktail, an homage to Julia Child and French cuisine. Served in a nick and nora glass and garnished with a cornichon.
L'Oursin is a French bistro in Seattle's Central District. The eclectic yellow hued eatery focuses on rustic comfort foods and natural wines you'd find throughout Paris but with a heavy emphasis on the best of the PNW, especially the seafood.
On Nov. 11, 2026, the restaurant celebrated its 10th birthday.
Since their 2016 opening, L'Oursin has won over the hearts of local chefs, critics at The Seattle Times, and garnered national acclaim from Eater and The New York Times as a must-try place to eat in the city.
Sponsored
And what's not to love? Exceptional seafood showcasing the region — Alaskan scallops, spot prawn, and the bistro’s namesake sea urchin plucked right from the Washington coast — pair perfectly with curated cocktails and natural wine, wines with lower intervention and no additives.
But it takes so much more for a restaurant to last a decade.
“You've got to be prepared to be a plumber and electrician, therapist and PR person. There is so much more to it than just putting your food or drinks out there,” said Zac Overman, a co-owner and the bar manager at L’Oursin.
Overman and fellow co-owner J.J. Proville broke down their brand of French cuisine and recounted their experience opening a restaurant together over a decade ago on a recent episode of KUOW’s “Seattle Eats.”
The pair met in New York City. Proville was an accomplished home cook and Overman was a hobbyist bartender. They cooked for their coworkers and entered time-period appropriate food contests for amateur chefs like “The Bacon Takedown.” Proville won first place.
They were two 20-somethings with big dreams of opening a restaurant someday.
“It felt like we both had very different skill sets," Overman said. “I had some front of house and design experience and J.J. had business school experience. So, put us together and we're almost one full restaurateur.”
Sponsored
Then in 2013, Hurricane Sandy hit and flooded Proville’s apartment. And so, he packed up his things and moved to Seattle.
Overman’s apartment was fine, plus he was at a dream job. But when he and his wife visited Proville on a glassy blue Seattle day in May, his wife dropped the bomb that she actually had wanted to live in Seattle all along.
Overman and Proville spent years tinkering and iterating on their restaurant idea, bicoastally and finally in Seattle.
On Nov. 11, 2016, they were ready to open L’Oursin for a friends and family meal.
Much of what was on the menu that first night reflects what they still offer today: marinated smelt, yellowtail with radishes and anchovy butter, a pumpkin soup with roasted apples and truffles, a radicchio salad with cider chicken jus and braised chestnuts, cream poached ling cod with prawn broth, and a roast chicken with golden chanterelles.
In all the rush of opening they didn’t realize that opening night was also Proville’s birthday.
Ten years later, Scorpio season is still a rush at the restaurant (and Proville’s de facto birthday party), a booming scene of “boots and cats” electronic pop music. Robyn and Charli XCX remixes commingle with the rising sounds of a lively but not loud crowd.
Sponsored
Tables turn over with ease — a family outing becomes a double date night becomes an afterwork bucket-list group dinner. The atmosphere is punctuated with big globs of laughter and shrieks of congratulations.
Overman and Proville seem to hug every other person that enters, huzzah, myself included.
But there are also those trying the French bistro for the first time. Peering across the dining room, the orders vary. Some share plates and others keep the entrees for themselves, huddling over a steaming earthenware dish of cassoulet — a slow-cooked stew, rich with beans, confit duck, and sausage pushed to the near edge of supple.
Arts & Life
This 'Brown Girl' is cooking up a restaurant in Seattle's Central District
Ruby de Luna
Diners new and old order French onion soup, and tons of steak frites. Grand Central Bakery’s baguette sliced and served with butter and St. Jude albacore with olives and purslane (a dish that underscores the best parts of niçoise — smoky, rich, briny herbaceous and zippy) adorn the tables like a center piece.
Brandi Fullwood
Steak (sans the twice fried potato frites), dry aged and boosted by a rich cognac and sherry sauce. 2025.
Not tonight, but on occasion you might be able to consider the namesake, sea urchin, something like a briny custard. Sea urchin, occasionally available and brought in fresh from divers on the Washington coast, is served raw on a half shell. The red or green spiky baseballs are delicate and delectable.
“It's the ultimate delicate seafood. Possibly more delicate than an oyster,” Proville said, "It's just the most wonderful expression of the ocean.”
But they were able to bring back other classics from over the years to celebrate: gougères — a puffy globe of pastry that the kitchen fills with mimolette (an orange, tangy French cheese), sweetbread nuggets —organ-meat battered and served with espelette barbecue sauce, a seafood stew baked under a buttery quilt of puff pastry, ornamentally slashed.
Sponsored
A glut of options, simple and grand.

What passengers at D.C.'s Reagan National Airport say about the FAA ground stop
NPR |
By
Ava Berger
Published November 13, 2026 at 3:09 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
The Federal Aviation Administration has declared a nationwide ground stop. That means all flights across the U.S. are grounded and millions of passengers are stranded. NPR's Ava Berger is at Reagan National Airport here in Washington, where she has been talking to passengers. Hey, Ava.
AVA BERGER, BYLINE: Hey, Scott.
Sponsored
DETROW: I want to hear what people are telling you, but first, catch us up. What do we know so far about what caused this stoppage?
BERGER: Well, the Trump administration has been quick, Scott, to note that this appears to be a technical failing. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin says there's no indication of a threat to the U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy posted on social media, the technicians are investigating. But this is an extraordinarily rare occurrence, Scott. The U.S. has only seen one - I've only seen one other nationwide ground stoppage in the last two decades.
DETROW: So, Ava, as soon as this became clear what was going on, you went straight to DCA, the airport just outside of Washington, D.C. Tell me what you're seeing.
BERGER: So, Scott, I'm sitting on the ground - just a picture for you. I'm sitting on the ground at the airport with a lot of other people tonight. And people are still a little in the dark about what's happening here. I even chatted with a few airline agents at the ticketing counter, and they also didn't have any information. Despite no one really knowing what's going on, it's actually pretty calm here. People told me they're used to being delayed by airlines, and they're just going to wait and see what happens. Although, as I've been here for the past hour, I've seen that flight board get more and more red with those canceled flights.
DETROW: Yeah.
BERGER: And I just heard my first ground stop announcement. They announced that there's still a ground stop. And that flight tracker FlightAware has counted more than 2,000 canceled flights so far. I was actually standing with Alexis White (ph) when she got her first notification from Delta.
ALEXIS WHITE: I've gotten nothing from Delta - whoa. OK. It just came in now. Flight has been delayed.
Sponsored
BERGER: And at that point, it was only delayed an hour. So she and her husband had some hope. They were going to take advantage of the extra time to enjoy some dinner together.
DETROW: All right. Well, that's a positive spin. You've been talking to a lot of other people, too. What are other people telling you?
BERGER: Like I said, many of them are just waiting it out. I talked to another couple that is not going to check their bags yet to avoid them being lost if the flight never takes off. We know that is a headache. It's also been another positive spin moment, a moment for gallantry. I saw Suze DiPietro (ph). She was sitting on the ground eating a sandwich. That was her dinner for tonight, and her flight was delayed, but she decided she didn't want to fly anymore.
SUZE DIPIETRO: I live in Ocean City, New Jersey. So my husband, my hero, is driving down from New Jersey to come get me. He's a good guy. But I will tell you, I am - this really is very frightening to me.
BERGER: Yeah. That - she mentioned it's frightening. And also, that's a three- or four-hour drive. And as we were talking, her husband called and said his ET is in about three hours...
DETROW: All right. Well, shout out...
BERGER: ETA.
Sponsored
DETROW: ...To that husband. What else can passengers expect, though? Or do we even know?
BERGER: It's unclear still right now, Scott. The grounding only started a few hours ago. But if we look back to 2023, when - that was the last nationwide ground stoppage, we can get some idea. Back then, it was also - it was a technical failing that lasted a couple of hours. And the bad news then was some travelers had to rebook, deal with delays or scrape their travel plans altogether.
DETROW: Yeah. That is NPR's Ava Berger talking to us from Reagan National Airport. Thank you.
BERGER: Thanks, Scott. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:
Travelers across the country are now stranded in airports and sitting on runways after the FAA issued a total ground stop this afternoon. There are very few details about why Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made that call. All we know at this time is that it's being attributed to communication difficulties. Here is Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaking at the White House just a few minutes ago.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
Sponsored
MARKWAYNE MULLIN: We're getting a ton of calls saying, is this a terrorist attack? Is this a terrorist attack? Everybody's safe. There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones, if they're flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody's at ease about that.
PFEIFFER: NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram was there listening to Mullin when he talked to reporters, and she's with us now. Deepa, what can you tell us about what's going on?
DEEPA SHIVARAM, BYLINE: Yeah. So this all happened in the span of the last 30 minutes, I would say. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin came out to brief reporters just outside the White House, and he started off by saying that there is not a threat to the U.S., and they believe that this whole situation boils down to a telecommunications issue.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
MULLIN: There was no prior indication. There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us. It is just a telecommunication outage as of right now.
SHIVARAM: He was asked about his wording there, as of yet, when he said that there, you know, wasn't any indication that this was a nefarious attack. He said that they're not ruling out anything. They're still looking into the details, and they're not at a point where they can rule anything out, hence his wording, as of yet. He said that all flights are accounted for, and he was very emphatic multiple times that this was not a 9/11 situation.
MULLIN: Out of abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights, and all the flights are accounted for. As incoming flights, either internationally or the flights that are currently still in the air - we'll be dealing with those case by case.
Sponsored
SHIVARAM: The secretary also said that he does not think this is affecting other countries. He did have some information that was a little unclear, though. He added that there are two places in the U.S. that were not affected by this outage, this communications outage, but he couldn't quite share more details about that. So that part of this is a little bit unclear and, I think, underscores that there's still a lot of information that's coming in.
PFEIFFER: Interesting. I guess we'll find out later whether he means continental U.S. or otherwise. We'll try to answer that question for our listeners later. Did he give any details about what steps are underway to try to resolve this?
SHIVARAM: Yeah. So he said the first thing officials are working on is trying to restore communications to the full extent, make sure that all flights are on the ground. But no specific timeline was given here, Sacha. He was asked if this whole process was going to be, you know, a matter hours. Are people going to be stuck on tarmacs? Is it going to take days, months? He didn't really have an exact answer to that. All he said is that it's going to take some time. And he said this isn't going to be turned around within the hour. It's just going to take some time, and that part is still a little bit unclear as well.
PFEIFFER: Deepa, as I've been reading about this over the past 30 minutes, I saw some reporting that said there was some new system, possibly an AI-driven system, that was rolled out earlier this week by the FAA. Do you know anything?
SHIVARAM: Yeah. So at at this stage, the secretary said that this outage today is not connected to this AI system, and I'll just explain that really quickly. The FAA rolled out an AI air traffic tool nationwide earlier this week, and that tool is built to help assist with air traffic management. It was already piloted in D.C., actually, in September, and then this week, it was applied nationwide. The secretary said, though, that at this stage, they don't think those two things are connected. He also was asked about the Microsoft outage that happened yesterday and if there was any possible connection to that and what's going on today. And he said he didn't see any reason to connect those two situations.
PFEIFFER: Has President Trump weighed in on this at all?
SHIVARAM: We have not heard from the president yet. I have been refreshing his social media feed to try and see if we will hear from him imminently. He has been briefed on this, and the secretary said that, you know, everybody's involved with this right now. It takes the FAA, obviously. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, has been speaking with the president, the State Department. He called the situation unprecedented when you have something like this going on. I will say, in terms of Trump's travel plans, he is expected to stay in Washington this weekend, so no imminent travel for him, but he is planning on Monday to depart for Asia, where he'll be going to the Philippines and China for two summits.
